**Other holdings and ventures**
- Lupin, CRISIL, Metro Brands, Star Health, Tata Motors and others. He set up RARE Enterprises in 2003. — [ThePrint profile](https://theprint.in/theprint-profile/rakesh-jhunjhunwala-was-investor-with-midas-touch-who-never-gave-up-on-indian-markets/1654819); [Business Today](https://www.businesstoday.in/markets/stocks/story/rakesh-jhunjhunwala-death-portfolio-stocks-tata-motors-titan-star-health-344609-2022-08-14)
- He co-founded Akasa Air with Vinay Dube and Aditya Ghosh. It launched in August 2022, about a week before his death. His stake was reported at about 40%. — [ThePrint](https://theprint.in/india/indias-warren-buffett-the-man-with-the-midas-touch-who-was-rakesh-jhunjhunwala/1082239); [Business Standard](https://www.business-standard.com/amp/article/markets/rakesh-jhunjhunwala-s-near-4-bn-stock-holdings-in-focus-after-death-122081600674_1.html) (single source for the 40%)

**Losses**
- A2Z Maintenance: 21% for about ₹20 crore in 2006. At the 2010 IPO he sold more than 1 million shares at ₹400 (over ₹40 crore), then bought 1.375 million after listing at ₹350.77 (about ₹48 crore), and 2.65 million at ₹100 in May 2012. By April 2013 the stock was down 94% at ₹19.45. Debt went from ₹405 crore to more than ₹1,100 crore, and the company went to corporate debt restructuring (CDR). He resigned as director in 2012. — [Outlook Business, "Spectacular bust"](https://www.outlookbusiness.com/markets/trend/spectacular-bust-321)
- In his words, he "misjudged the quality and character of the entrepreneur" in A2Z and Bilcare. He "put in an additional ₹70 crore" in A2Z and later sold at ₹10-11. — [Outlook Business interview](https://www.outlookbusiness.com/interview/you-cant-make-money-on-borrowed-knowledge-566)
- 2008: his portfolio was reportedly down about 30% and not recovered until about 2012. — [Holistic Investment (blog)](https://www.holisticinvestment.in/rakesh-jhunjhunwala-net-worth-investing-lessons/). WEAK SOURCE: the drawdown is widely reported as larger, but I found no reliable figure.

`insight:spiva-india-2025` | confidence: verified | date: 2026-03-15

S&P Dow Jones Indices SPIVA India Year-End 2025 scorecard (benchmarks now S&P India LargeMidCap for large-cap funds, S&P India SmallCap for mid/small-cap, S&P India BMI for ELSS). Large-cap funds: underperformance 75.0% (1 yr), 74.2% (3 yr), 84.4% (5 yr), 76.3% (10 yr). In 2025 the benchmark rose 8.9% vs 7.3% equal-weighted / 9.4% asset-weighted for funds. Mid/small-cap funds: 12.1% (1 yr), 41.5% (3 yr), 46.0% (5 yr), 79.0% (10 yr) - 2025 was their best relative year since 2014 as the S&P India SmallCap fell 7.9% while funds lost only 0.7%/0.3% (defensive cash/quality tilts help in falling small-cap markets). ELSS: 55.0%, 58.5% and 82.9% underperformance over 3, 5 and 10 years. Mid-year 2025 report (to Jun-2025): 73% large-cap and 82% mid/small-cap underperformed over 10 years. SPIVA adjusts for survivorship (merged/liquidated funds count as losers). Lessons: (1) in Indian large caps, after costs, 3 in 4 professionals lose to a cheap index over a decade - large-cap stock picking is the hardest place to add value; (2) mid/small-cap active managers do better in down years but still mostly lose over 10 years; (3) short-run outperformance (1-yr) is a poor guide to persistence. Actionable: our personal stock picks must be benchmarked against a Nifty 50/LargeMidcap index fund and a quality factor index, net of taxes and costs, with records kept honestly (Buffett 1993: the know-nothing indexer beats most professionals).

Sources:
- https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/documents/spiva/spiva-india-scorecard-year-end-2025.pdf
- https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/spiva/article/spiva-india-year-end-2025/
- https://cafemutual.com/news/industry/35917-73-of-indian-large-cap-and-82-of-mid-and-small-cap-funds-have-underperformed-sp-india-benchmarks-over-a-10-year-period

`insight:flag-pledge-severity` · verified

RULE: our disqualifier (pledge >25% of promoter holding or rising) stays the DEFAULT; an override must be written down as a decision record. Grade severity on six questions: (1) PURPOSE: disclosed and specific (family debt from a known investment, funding the listed company's own rights issue) vs undisclosed or to fund other group companies; (2) SIZE: % of promoter holding and % of total equity, plus the price cushion before margin calls; (3) TREND: falling via actual stake sales or repayments (Apollo Hospitals: ~76% in 2019 -> ~2% by Aug 2025 after block sales) vs rising while price rises (Zee/Essel 59% -> ~90%); (4) LENDER: banks with long tenor vs NBFCs/MFs with loan-against-shares and short tenor (2018-19 IL&FS freeze turned MF pledges into fire sales); (5) LISTED-COMPANY LEVERAGE: is the company itself unlevered and cash-generative, or does it also guarantee group debt; (6) GROUP HISTORY: any past invocations, diversion or contagion (ADAG, Essel, Future, Cox & Kings = severe). A pledge that is high but falling, disclosed, bank-funded, at the family level, in a clean group with an unlevered company is a sizing and monitoring issue; a rising pledge with undisclosed purpose in a group with a history is a disqualifier. Also treat non-disposal undertakings and 'encumbrances' as pledges. HONEST CAVEAT: even benign pledges are reflexive in a crash; Apollo worked partly because the price rose. Size such positions small and track quarterly SAST disclosures.

body:
- **Physical output from BRSR intensity ratios** (new technique). BRSR gives total energy (193,212 GJ) and "energy intensity per unit of physical output" (1.3060 GJ/unit), where the unit is "number of equivalent units manufactured/assembled" `[AR26 BRSR P6]`. Units = 193,212 ÷ 1.3060 = **~147,900 equivalent units in FY26** (FY25: 200,812 ÷ 1.4538 = ~138,100).
- **Check:** water 179,627 kL ÷ 1.2142 kL/unit = 147,939, and waste 7,796.5 t ÷ 0.0527 = 147,941, the same number. This confirms the *arithmetic* only, not the definition (all three share one denominator).
- **Volume vs price.** Units +7.1% against revenue +17.4%, so **realisation/mix per equivalent unit ≈ +9.6%** (₹7.49 lakh → ₹8.21 lakh) [EST]. *Caveat:* "equivalent units" is a company weighting; we cannot tell whether a QSK60 counts as one unit or many.
- **Utilisation:** "70% utilisation" (an analyst repeating management, not contradicted) `[CC-Q4FY26]`. Implied capacity ≈ 147.9k ÷ 0.70 ≈ **~210k equivalent units** [EST]. Headroom ≈ 40% more volume before major capex. That fits management's "no major capital expenditure plan" `[CC-Q4FY26]`.
- **The binding constraint is not CIL's plants.** It is *HHP engines made elsewhere*: QSK60 at CTIPL, and QSK95 imported, made "largely in the US" `[CC-Q4FY26]`. Allocation is global ("demand is outpacing the addition of capacity" `[CC-Q1FY27]`). **Utilisation at CIL's own plants therefore tells you little about DC growth.** Watch CMI's capacity statements instead (an analyst cited "$450 m to raise 20 GW by 2030" `[CC-Q4FY26]`, unverified).

**Rule (from the task):** take `research_notes/Backtests/india_pead_live/universe.csv` (1,547 symbols); drop financials, banks,
NBFCs and insurers; keep ₹1,000–20,000 cr market cap; shuffle with Python `random.Random(20261123).shuffle`; walk the list. The **first** company that passes
the stage-2 hard filters becomes the subject.

**How it was run** (scripts in the scratchpad `live_dd1/scripts/sel1.py`, `sel2.py`):
1. **Market cap** = `shares` (universe.csv) × NSE close on **20-Nov-2026** (bhavcopy `sec_bhavdata_full_20112026.csv`, the
   latest published file; the 21-Nov and 23-Nov files were not yet available). Every one of the 1,547 symbols had a price. **810** were in ₹1,000–20,000 cr.
2. **Financials removed.** Two sources were used. (a) The NSE index files `ind_niftytotalmarket_list.csv` + `ind_niftymicrocap250_list.csv`, industry
   = "Financial Services": 29 names (AAVAS APTUS BAJAJHLDNG CAMS CANFINHOME CHOICEIN CREDITACC CSBBANK DCBBANK EDELWEISS
   EQUITASBNK FEDFINA HOMEFIRST IEX IFCI IIFLCAPS J&KBANK JMFINANCIL KFINTECH KTKBANK PAISALO RELIGARE SAMMAANCAP SBFC
   SHAREINDIA SOUTHBANK TMB UJJIVANSFB UTIAMC). (b) 484 in-range names had no index industry. Among them I classified 40 by hand as
   financial (lenders, brokers, rating agencies, investment holding companies): 5PAISA AFSL ARMANFIN BFINVEST CARERATING CONSOFINVT CREST DHANBANK
   ESAFSFB FUSION GEOJITFSL IBULLSLTD ICRA INDIASHLTR INDOSTAR JSWHL KICL MAHSCOOTER MASFIN MONARCH MUFIN MUTHOOTMF NSIL PFS
   PILANIINVS PNBGILTS PRIMESECU PRUDENT PSB REPCOHOME SATIN SMCGLOBAL SPANDANA SUMMITSEC SURYODAY TFCILTD TSFINV UGROCAP
   UTKARSHBNK VHL. This left **741 eligible names**. They were sorted alphabetically, then `random.Random(20261123).shuffle`d.
3. **Order drawn (first 10):** NRBBEARING, VSTIND, HINDWAREAP, **SUNFLAG**, QUESS, ASHAPURMIN, ROUTE, RAMCOIND, OAL, POKARNA.

1. **Annual reports are a disclosure-quality instrument more than a promise ledger.** Their forward text is mostly undated. The signals that work are stale dates at filing, sentences copied year to year, unchanged quantities, and assets that disappear from tables. Proposal: feed these flags into the stage-2/4 governance soft flags (they are objective and cheap).
2. **Do not compare AR-mode MCS with concall MCS.** The universe of statements differs: no Q&A, no numbers, no prompting.
3. **Next:**
   - Widen the zone to the overview pages and the BRSR "specific commitments" row, then re-measure recall.
   - Add present-tense plan patterns ("is expanding ... by launching").
   - Run the LLM step (`--emit-prompts`, then `llm_extract.py` on the AR cache root) and compare with the rule builder.
   - Re-check Bajna EC when Sunflag files again (live call 4).
